key_insight: Activation probes are a promising misuse-detection tool but fail when production inputs shift from short to long contexts; this work develops probe designs and training strategies that generalize across that shift, making probes practical for deployment.
problem_solved: Fixes the failure mode where activation probes trained on short-context data break down on long-context inputs common in production, preventing reliable misuse detection.
method: Design context-aware probe architectures that aggregate and attend over long activation sequences so signals remain stable as context length grows.
Train with shift-aware data augmentation (mixing short and long contexts) and objectives that emphasize robustness to distributional change (e.g., contrastive/regularized losses and calibration).
Evaluate and iterate on probe decision thresholds and calibration under realistic production shifts to maintain precision/recall trade-offs.
impact: Makes activation-based misuse detection robust to real-world long-context usage, enabling safer deployment of frontier LMs by reducing degradation in detection performance when input distributions change.
visual_elements: Schematic comparing short-context vs long-context inputs and where probes read activations (showing failure vs robust design).
Architecture diagram of a context-aware probe (aggregation/attention over token activations).
Line chart of detection performance (precision/recall or accuracy) vs context length for baseline probes and the proposed approach.

paper_authors: János Kramár, Joshua Engels, Zheng Wang, Bilal Chughtai, Rohin Shah
